https://www.politico.eu/article/german-c.text: The German government could help Kyiv with bringing men of military age who reside in the country back to Ukraine, said Foreign Affairs Minister Johann Wadephul. In an interview with Paul Ronzheimer of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network released Wednesday , Wadephul said Berlin could share its data on Ukrainian men with German residency permits. “We know who lives here. For example, who receives social benefits or who is registered here,” said Wadephul. On the basis of this data, these men could “be contacted by the Ukrainian government and called upon.” The whole process, however, should run “without coercion,” added the minister. Advertisement Advertisement Approximately 1 million Ukrainian refugees obtained a temporary residence permit in Germany following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, including around 450,000 men , according to official 2025 data. Ukraine has been under martial law since February 2022, prohibiting men aged 25 to 60 who are eligible for military service from leaving the country . Approximately 1.17 million adult Ukrainian men are currently benefiting from temporary protection across the EU, and their presence abroad has been a matter of discussion between Kyiv, Brussels and EU capitals. German Chancellor Freidrich Merz urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in November 2025 to curb the flow of young men leaving Ukraine. And in April this year, Zelenskyy said in a press conference alongside Merz that the return of men of fighting age was “a matter of fairness.” In July, the EU banned men of fighting age from its refugee scheme in response to “the evolving military needs of Ukraine.” The ban only covers new applicants, and not men already residing in the EU. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network is a multi-publication initiative publishing scoops, investigations, interviews, op-eds and analysis that reverberate across the world. It connects journalists from Axel Springer brands—including POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, and Onet— on major stories for an international audience. Their ambitious reporting stretches across Axel Springer platforms: online, print, TV, and audio. Together, the outlets reach hundreds of millions of people worldwide.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9dw.text: Figure caption, Watch: Crews race to rescue passengers from burning ferry in Philippines By Virma Simonette Rivera ,Â Reporting from Manila Â and Â Kelly Ng Published 11 September 2026, 05:23 BST Updated 07:33 BST More than 40 hours after a deadly ferry fire began, Philippine rescuers have boarded the charred remains of the MV June Aster in search of dozens of missing people. Five people been found dead, while 43 people have been rescued, many of whom are receiving treatment in hospital. Eighty-four people remain missing. Photos shared by the Philippine Coast Guard on Friday morning showed smoke still curling from the ferry, which had been travelling from the capital Manila to the island of Coron - though the plumes appear to have died down in fresh photos from Friday afternoon. Officials struggled to board the hull since operations began on Wednesday because of the toxic fumes and heat. Image source, Philippine Coast Guard Image caption, Photos shared by the coastguard on Friday morning show smoke still curling from the MV June Aster They finally got on at about 11:30 local time (03:30 GMT) on Friday, the coast guard said. "The biggest challenge for us really is to penetrate the ship [as] there is still a visible, thick smoke," the coastguard's spokeswoman Noemie Cayabyab told the BBC earlier. "No matter how we try to push through, high temperatures and toxic smoke remain a severe risk to our personnel," she told local media earlier. Smoke resulting from incomplete burning contains dense, lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide. Earlier, authorities reported that 86 were still unaccounted for, but as of Friday morning, the figure stood at 84 â two passengers whose names were on the ship's manifest did not go onboard, authorities say. Rescuers have widened their search area, Cayabyab says, adding that the coastguard has deployed one of its largest ships and done radio broadcasts to vessels in the area. The search teams are also accompanied by divers and nurses. A local diver in Coron told the BBC on Friday that he and his team were on standby to help out and awaiting instructions from the coast guard. The coast guard also conducted an aerial survey of waters near the disaster site. Image source, Philippine Coast Guard Image caption, Rescuers have widened their search area on Friday, authorities say The plan is to resume firefighting efforts, first from the cargo hold of the ferry, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, Cayabyab said. Earlier, the coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that was where the fire started. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted. A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat had described the frantic cries on board the passenger-cargo vessel when the fire erupted on Wednesday evening. Roland Lerma recalled falling while scrambling to get off the burning boat. "When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," the 30-year-old told the BBC. He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea. Lerma said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark. "It was cold [in the sea] If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," he said. The ferry, which set off from Manila, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, in the province of Palawan, when it caught fire. The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident. The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported. Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry. "Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text: Good morning. Children and young people are at the top of the agenda today, with the publication of a hard-hitting report from Dame Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England, and a Times article by Andy Burnham. They are focusing on slightly different cohorts – Burnham is writing about young people who leave school and enter the benefits system, while the de Souza reports covers the experiences of young children in multiple aspects of their lives – but their overall message is the same: the younger generation is being let down. De Souza has studied more than 160 datasets to examine how what happens to children as they grow up varies across England and she says the variation is “staggering”. In her report, The Childhood Lottery, she explains: In four local authorities, the total amount spent on youth services per teenager is the princely sum of £0, £421 less than in the highest spending local authority.
